planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Paniculata grows noticeably larger and more vigorously than typical summersweet selections, so allow extra room in the border or woodland edge.

directions: Paniculata is an older, extra-vigorous form of the native shade shrub summersweet, building into a taller, wider colony than most named clethra cultivars over time. Its late-summer flower spikes carry unusually large, heavy panicles of small white blooms, giving a denser, showier display of the species' trademark sweet fragrance than the compact modern selections bred for small gardens. Because of its size, it works best as a background planting along a shaded fence line, stream bank, or woodland edge rather than a tight foundation bed. Keep soil consistently moist and acidic; established plants spread slowly by suckering to form a broad multi-stemmed thicket.

common_name: Bees Sunset Red Hot Poker (Golden-Apricot Bicolor Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, sandy, humus-enriched soil in full sun; good drainage is essential year-round, since Bees Sunset rots quickly in soggy winter soil.

directions: Bees Sunset carries slender, tapering flower spikes that open a rich golden yellow heavily streaked with deep apricot-orange, giving each torch a warm, two-toned glow rather than the single flat color of many older red hot poker selections. Bronze-tinted stems rise well above a low base of gray-green, grassy foliage, blooming steadily from early into late summer and drawing hummingbirds throughout the display. This selection traces to the historic English nursery Bees of Chester, one of the sources of many classic Kniphofia hybrids still grown today. Site in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, and tie foliage over the crown before hard frost in colder zones to protect it through winter.

common_name: Timothy Red Hot Poker (Coral-Pink AGM Torch Lily)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Timothy is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once established and holds its RHS Award of Garden Merit bloom quality even in lean, dry sites.

directions: Timothy sends up bronze-flushed flower stalks topped with dense, tapering spikes of dark coral-pink tubular flowers that gradually fade to cream as they age, stretching the bloom season from midsummer well into fall longer than many single-flush poker cultivars. This Award of Garden Merit selection stays clumping rather than spreading, with narrow, arching foliage that remains tidy through the growing season. It pairs well with silver-leaved companions like lavender or artemisia, which echo its bronze stem tones. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun; Timothy tolerates considerable heat and dry spells once its roots are established, but resents standing winter moisture around the crown.

common_name: Border Ballet Red Hot Poker (Dusty Coral Succulent-Leaved Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Border Ballet's thick, nearly succulent evergreen foliage keeps the clump attractive even when the plant is out of bloom.

directions: Border Ballet, selected at the noted plantsman's garden Western Hills Nursery in California, produces soft, dusty coral-colored torches on tall stems that continue opening steadily from June through August rather than in one short burst. Its foliage is thicker and more succulent-looking than typical grassy Kniphofia leaves, giving the clump structural presence in the border even between bloom flushes. The cultivar is propagated by division rather than seed to preserve its distinctive muted coral tone, since seed-grown Kniphofia often segregates into a wider color range. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun and avoid winter-wet sites, where the fleshy crown is prone to rot.

common_name: Nancy's Red Red Hot Poker (Dwarf Coral-Red Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Nancy's Red is a genuinely dwarf poker, so it suits the front of a border where taller Kniphofia cultivars would crowd out neighboring perennials.

directions: Nancy's Red is a compact, low-growing poker that opens brick-red buds into slender, cone-shaped spikes of dusky coral-red florets tipped in creamy yellow, the flowers nodding gradually downward as they age and mature seed. Its narrow, grassy foliage stays low and tidy, well under the height of standard border pokers, making it useful for edging a hot-colored bed or planting in gravel gardens where larger Kniphofia would overwhelm the scale. It flowers reliably from midsummer into late summer and draws hummingbirds and bees during that window. Grow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid rich, wet ground that encourages rot at the crown.

common_name: Prince Igor Red Hot Poker (Towering Orange-and-Yellow Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Prince Igor throws up exceptionally tall flower spikes, so site it toward the back of the border or as a bold vertical specimen with room overhead.

directions: Prince Igor is among the tallest garden red hot pokers commonly grown, sending flower spikes to six or seven feet above a clump of arching gray-green foliage. The spikes open a bold solid orange, and as the lower florets finish and drop away the exposed base of the flower head turns bright yellow, so a single mature spike briefly displays both colors in bands. It was distributed through the English plantswoman Beth Chatto's nursery and remains a favorite for gardeners wanting real height and drama from a hardy perennial rather than a tender exotic. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun with wind shelter for the tall stems, and divide crowded clumps every few years to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Bressingham Comet Red Hot Poker (Compact Fine-Leaved Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; in USDA zones 5 and 6 tie the foliage together over the crown in late fall and mulch to shed winter moisture and protect against hard freezes.

directions: Bressingham Comet, a Blooms of Bressingham introduction from England, forms a compact clump of very fine, grass-like foliage well under a foot tall, from which bare stems rise to display short, dense flower racemes in bright orange tipped with red that age gracefully to yellow. Its small stature and narrow leaves give it a more refined, airy texture than bulkier red hot poker cultivars, letting it slot into rock gardens and smaller mixed borders where full-size pokers would look out of scale. Blooms open over the main summer season and continue drawing hummingbirds for weeks. Grow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and protect the crown from standing winter water, which is the most common cause of loss in this genus.
